Intel's FY2025 10-K states that the company has "delayed or cancelled manufacturing facility construction or expansion projects in Ohio, Germany, Poland, Malaysia and Israel and initiated the consolidation of our assembly and test facility in Costa Rica into our other facilities," while the FY2024 10-K reported delays in those same locations, focusing on the high fixed cost structure of Intel's manufacturing operations and the risk of underutilized capacity [1][2]. Both filings warn of impairment charges from underutilized assets, but the FY2025 filing reports that in 2025 and 2024 Intel recorded "$950 million and $3.3 billion, respectively, of charges related to non-cash impairments and the accelerated depreciation for certain manufacturing assets that were determined to have no remaining or reduced operational use," while the FY2024 filing reported that "in the third quarter of 2024 we recorded $3.1 billion of charges related to non-cash impairments and the accelerated depreciation for certain manufacturing assets, a substantial majority of which related to the Intel 7 process node [1][2]."

The FY2025 10-K introduces a prominent threshold risk tied specifically to Intel 14A: if Intel is unable to secure a significant external foundry customer for that node it may pause or discontinue its pursuit of next-generation leading-edge process technologies, and Intel has been unsuccessful to date in securing any significant external foundry customers for any of its nodes, with prospects for Intel 14A described as uncertain [1][3]. The FY2024 filing describes the difficulty of attracting foundry customers to Intel's external foundry business and warns that Intel may not be successful in developing a competitive foundry business for external customers with respect to either leading-edge or mature process nodes, which would make it difficult to realize a favorable return on investments in process technology and manufacturing capacity [4][5].

The FY2025 10-K catalogues consequences of a potential pause or discontinuation of Intel 14A, including that Intel's products business would become dependent on TSMC, with which Intel has no long-term contract, noting that "most of our competitors have longer and more established relationships with TSMC and other third-party foundries than we do [3]." The FY2025 filing warns that pausing Intel 14A could trigger "significant material impairments" on the over $100 billion of property, plant and equipment, net on Intel's balance sheet as of December 27, 2025, "the substantial majority of which" relates to the foundry business, and would likely result in discontinuing the new Ohio fabrication facilities under construction [6]. The FY2025 10-K further warns that a pause could cause Intel to lose eligibility for government incentives and require repayment of amounts already received, and could require "substantial additional payments" to SCIP partners if construction and wafer commitments cannot be met, while the FY2024 filing presents SCIP exposure as a general financing risk illustrated by a $755 million charge in the fourth quarter of 2024 for Ireland SCIP construction delays [5][6][7].

Intel's FY2025 10-K also stresses that a pause or discontinuation of Intel 14A "may materially adversely impact our ability to hire and retain key talent across our foundry organization," and warns that potential Intel 18A-P customers who doubt Intel's commitment to Intel 14A "may be inclined to remain with their current foundry partners [8]." The FY2025 filing characterizes any such decision as "effectively irreversible" given the "decades of significant continuous investments in R&D, talent accumulation, intellectual property, state-of-the-art facilities and technical know-how needed to compete in leading-edge node design, development and manufacturing," emphasizing that the barriers to restarting a leading-edge node program, once abandoned, would be nearly insurmountable [8].
